definition: The label your visual system gives to the mix of visible wavelengths (about 400–700 nm, photon energies 1.8–3.1 eV) reaching your eye; an object's color is the part of the incoming light it sends toward you.
The amount of light at each wavelength in a beam; most real light is a mixture of many wavelengths.
Color-sensing cells in the retina of three types, S, M, and L, with sensitivity peaks near 420, 534, and 564 nm.
Different spectra that produce the same three cone signals and therefore look the same color, such as 580 nm yellow and a red-plus-green mixture.
Combining colored lights (usually red, green, and blue); more light added means brighter, and all three together look white. Screens work this way.
Combining absorbers such as inks, paints, or filters (usually cyan, magenta, and yellow); each removes part of the spectrum, and all three together look black.
A molecule with a chain of alternating single and double bonds; longer chains have smaller electron energy gaps and absorb longer wavelengths, which is how many dyes and pigments get their color.
The energy gap between a solid's filled valence band and empty conduction band; photons with energy above Eg can be absorbed.
The wavelength 1240 eV·nm / Eg below which a semiconductor or insulator absorbs light strongly.

Eg above 3.1 eV: colorless and transparent; Eg below 1.8 eV: all visible light absorbed (opaque, dark or metallic); Eg between: only the blue end absorbed, so the material looks yellow, orange, or red.
The electric field of the ions surrounding a transition-metal ion in a crystal, which splits its d-orbital energies into gaps that can absorb visible light (as with Cr³⁺ in ruby).
Absorption of a photon by moving an electron from one ion to a neighboring ion, such as Fe²⁺ to Ti⁴⁺ in blue sapphire; it produces strong colors from trace impurities.
Scattering of light by particles much smaller than the wavelength, with intensity proportional to 1/λ⁴; it makes the sky blue and sunsets red.
Color produced by interference from structures about the size of light's wavelength (thin films, layered nanostructures) rather than by pigment absorption.
Reinforcement or cancellation of light reflected from the front and back surfaces of a thin layer; the result depends on thickness, index, and viewing angle.
Color that changes with viewing angle, typical of structural color in soap bubbles, oil slicks, and butterfly wings.
A material that absorbs light (often blue or UV) and re-emits it at a longer wavelength; white LEDs use a yellow phosphor on a blue LED.
